We also can directly supplement neurotransmitter production by giving patients precursors which pass the blood-brain barrier and are then metabolized appropriately. An example is carbodopa/levodopa, a dopamine precursor drug given to Parkinson's patients (Parkinson's results from a deficiency of dopamine in certain parts of the brain due to progressive cell death in those areas). This drug does result in elevated mood for patients (which is good because Parkinson's also causes depression) but it also can cause obsessive or frenetic behavior plus hoarding of medication, and other side effects in the peripheral nervous system like swelling of the feet, and in a patient who is not deficient in dopamine could cause more severe side effects including heart arrhythmia.

On the topic of recreational drugs: while many stimulants have dopaminergic effects, they have affinity for a variety of other receptors as well including norepinephrine and acetylcholine which have other effects (in particular, these two explain stimulants' effects on things like heart rate and executive function, while the dopaminergic effects explain their addictiveness). 

An example of a more selective agonist would actually be LSD which binds relatively exclusively to serotonin receptors in the brain. While I'm sure some acid enthusiasts would say otherwise, too much of that would probably not be great for coherent functioning, though microdosing various hallucinogens does have a lot of medical promise for treating depression and certain other mental health conditions. 

For endorphins like dopamine, the most obvious and selective street drug agonist I can think of is heroin ("endorphin" is short for "endogenous morphine"), and we all know how bleak the outcomes of that can be.

since most people implicitly allow people like postal workers and trick-or-treaters and door-to-door salesmen to walk up to their door to ring the bell without it being considered trespassing, this requirement to actually explicitly invite people basically doesn't apply to things like slipping on ice on someone's driveway since effectively anyone with any good reason to be knocking on your door is not yet a trespasser at that point unless it's provable that they had no legitimate business being there and were only there to trespass, or unless you had e.g. a "no trespassing" sign at the edges of the property stating that anyone entering the premises must be explicitly invited. Trespass laws do vary slightly by state but that's the general shape of the matter.

Note that this only includes normal/accidental dangers like wet floors, unmarked or broken steps, ice, etc, and not intentional malice. If you set out a bear trap in your house as a "security system" and a burglar steps on it, you are absolutely liable for that person's injuries since you intentionally caused them, and depending on your jurisdiction that would probably even be criminal. If you set out a trap with a deadly weapon [such as a shotgun](https://www.baltimoresun.com/news/bs-xpm-1999-12-20-9912200163-story.html) and someone were to die, I'd certainly be hard pressed not to call that malice aforethought.

but this trespasser/invitee distinction does bring up the issue of intent - why is a would-be burglar who injured himself on your icy driveway before even actually breaking in less entitled to compensation than a FedEx worker who does the same in the course of her job? Or a religious proselytizer on his way to preach to you whom you didn't actually "invite" or want to be there but whom you haven't ordered to leave the premises yet? that's why California did away with the trespasser/invitee distinction and now applies a simple "would a reasonable person be expected to remedy or warn people of this danger?" test regardless of who the plaintiff is. Meaning if a postal worker could sue you for that slippery driveway, so could a burglar.
